Fields per text: id (corpus text id), source_id (corpus.sqlite sources.id), title, blurb, english_source ('site_json' = web/data/texts/<id>.json lines, 'corpus_db' = translations table, author_type='model'), model, model_version, translated_on (YYYY-MM-DD), tags []. v2: categories[] (slug,title,blurb,app_mode?,explainer_html?,coming_soon[]) and per-text categories[] (slugs; a text may be in several, [] = uncategorised) and hooks[] (verbatim substrings of that text's machine English; build_static.py verifies them).

categories.title: Remedies
categories.blurb: Medical prescriptions from Assyrian and Babylonian healers: plants, oils, beer and the occasional incantation, with instructions for preparing and applying them. Editions are mostly in print (BAM). English here is an unedited machine draft, and drug and plant names are often wrong.

categories.title: Omens
categories.blurb: “If… then…” observations from Mesopotamian divination: birds, rivers, the moon and sun, dreams, births, and the entrails of sacrificed sheep. The English shown is an unedited machine draft, and many technical divination terms come out wrong.

categories.title: Epic Hunt
categories.blurb: Narrative and mythological fragments: gods in council, monsters defeated, floods and a goddess's self-praise. Most have only scholarly print editions. The English shown is an unedited machine draft.

categories.title: Math
categories.blurb: School and working mathematics from the 3rd to 1st millennium BCE: multiplication and reciprocal tables, squares, field and canal computations, and a gold-alloy problem. Numbers survive machine translation better than words, but the connecting English is an unedited machine draft.
categories.explainer_html:
Reading Babylonian numbers

Mesopotamian scribes counted in base 60 (sexagesimal). Each place is worth 60 times the place to its right, just as each decimal place is worth 10 times. So “1 15” means 1×60 + 15 = 75, and “8.00” (as written in the English below) means 8×60 = 480. The same notation is used for fractions: “30” after the units place means 30/60 = ½. Scribes usually did not mark where the units place was, so “1 15” could also mean 1¼ (1 + 15/60); the reader works it out from context. Base 60 survives in our 60 minutes and 360 degrees. A reciprocal table lists, for each number, the number that multiplies with it to make 60 (or 1): “reciprocal 4 and 15” means 4 × 15 = 60. Numbers such as 7 or 59 have no finite reciprocal in base 60, and the tables mark them as missing.

categories.title: Love & Fertility
categories.blurb: Rituals and recipes for restoring a man's desire (ŠÀ.ZI.GA, “rising of the heart”), and Babylonian love lyrics, several from the cult of Marduk and his consort Zarpanītu. These are fragmentary tablets known mainly from scholarly print editions, and the selection is small. The English is an unedited machine draft.

categories.title: Music
categories.blurb: Texts about making music in Mesopotamia: laments sung by the kalû-priests to drum and harp, a catalogue of the lamenters' repertoire, and an Old Babylonian liturgy with its song sections. The English is an unedited machine draft; instrument names (balaĝ = harp or drum; ub, lilis) are rendered inconsistently. The famous tuning and notation tablets have no transliteration in our corpus yet; they are listed below as coming soon.

coming_soon.note: A hymn to the goddess Nikkal with musical instructions below the text. Our corpus has its catalogue entry only; a transliteration is being sought.

coming_soon.title: KAR 158: catalogue of songs
coming_soon.note: A catalogue of song incipits grouped by genre and instrument. A transliteration is being sought.
